turns.human_input: I have a completed study on machine learning interpretability in clinical decision support — specifically how clinicians actually interact with SHAP explanations in practice. It's empirically strong: 18-month observational study in two hospitals, 47 clinician interviews, usage log analysis. I can write this up as a conference paper for NeurIPS or AAAI, or as a journal article for JAMIA or Journal of Biomedical Informatics. I'm not sure which route is better for this type of work. What should I be weighing?
turns.ai_response:
This is a consequential venue choice because your work spans two communities — ML/AI and biomedical informatics — that have genuinely different publication norms, citation structures, and what 'contribution' means.

The conference route (NeurIPS, AAAI) gives you speed, visibility in the ML community, and strong signal for AI-focused faculty positions or industry roles. NeurIPS in particular has dramatically expanded its scope toward human-AI interaction and interpretability evaluation — your empirical work on how SHAP functions in clinical practice could fit well in the main track or as a spotlight. The cost: conference papers are typically 8-10 pages, which will compress your 18-month observational study significantly. Reviewers from the ML community may also undervalue your qualitative methodology if it's not framed carefully around the ML contribution rather than the clinical workflow finding.

The journal route (JAMIA, JBI) gives you space — 6,000-10,000 words to do justice to your mixed-methods design — and positions this for the biomedical informatics and clinical informatics audience who are most likely to act on your findings. JAMIA specifically has been publishing strong HCI-adjacent and sociotechnical informatics work. The trade-off is time: journal review cycles in this space run 6-18 months, and the citation impact within the ML interpretability conversation will be slower.

A third path worth considering: a top HCI venue like CHI. Your 47-interview, observational design is exactly the kind of empirical work CHI values, and the interpretability-in-practice angle is a strong fit for their growing healthcare track.

What is your primary career trajectory — research faculty, industry AI, or clinical informatics? And is the 18-month timeframe a factor — do you need publications moving soon?

turns.human_input: I'm on the academic track aiming for a faculty position in a school of information or informatics. Timeline matters — I'm on the job market in 18 months. I've made my decision: I'm going with JAMIA. The audience fit is right, the prestige is right for the informatics faculty positions I'm targeting, and the space lets me do the study justice. What should I be thinking about for the submission itself?
turns.ai_response:
Good choice for your target positions. JAMIA is the right signal for informatics faculty searches, and at 18 months you have realistic runway for a journal cycle if you submit soon.

For the submission itself, the key things to optimize:

Article type: JAMIA publishes Research and Applications papers and Brief Communications. For an 18-month two-hospital study with 47 interviews plus log analysis, you want the full Research and Applications format — don't undersell the study by compressing it into a Brief Communication.

Structure and framing: JAMIA readers are clinicians, informaticists, and health IT researchers. Your abstract and introduction need to foreground the clinical decision support context and the practical implication — why does it matter that clinicians interact with SHAP explanations in this particular way? The ML methodological contribution (your evaluation of interpretability in situ) should be present but should serve the clinical framing, not lead it.

Mixed-methods reporting: JAMIA has published mixed-methods work but reviewers vary in comfort with qualitative components. Use a recognized reporting framework — COREQ for the interview component is standard and will preempt reviewer concerns about rigor. Explicitly state your integration approach for how the log analysis and interview findings were combined.

Conflict of interest and ethics: Make sure your IRB approval language is clear and covers both hospitals. JAMIA reviewers will check this carefully given clinical data.

Review timeline: JAMIA typically returns first decisions in 6-10 weeks. If you submit by month 1-2 of your 18-month window, a revision-and-resubmit cycle still leaves you room to have an accepted paper in hand before job applications go out. Do you have the manuscript in draft form already?

turns.ai_response:
Submit to CHI in parallel.

Your advisor's read is correct on two counts: CHI carries genuine weight in informatics and iSchool faculty searches — hiring committees in those programs value HCI conference publications explicitly, and a CHI paper signals methodological range in a way that a single JAMIA submission does not. More importantly, your 18-month observational study with 47 interviews is exactly the kind of empirical HCI work CHI values. The overlap is not dilution; it's the same study reaching two distinct communities who will cite it for different reasons.

The dual-track is legitimate here because you're not submitting the same paper to two venues — a CHI submission should be a distinct contribution focused on the human-computer interaction dimensions (how clinicians cognitively process SHAP visualizations, what explanation features drive trust or distrust, the breakdown moments in the interaction) while JAMIA gets the full sociotechnical and clinical informatics framing. They share a data source but should have different research questions foregrounded.

The overhead is real but finite: you need a CHI-length version (typically 10 pages ACM format) carved from your existing manuscript, re-framed around the HCI contribution. If your draft is in late stage, this is probably 2-3 weeks of focused rewriting rather than a parallel research effort.

The risk of not doing it: if JAMIA comes back with a major revision at month 4, you'll wish you had the CHI paper already in the pipeline. Having two tracks hedges your timeline risk on the job market. Do it.

Protecting the integrity of the contribution over the optics of a second line on the CV is the right instinct at your career stage.

For JAMIA-only strategy with the timeline risk in mind: the most practical hedge is to get the submission in as early as possible. Every week you spend polishing is a week off your runway. If the manuscript is in late draft, set a hard submission date within the next two to three weeks and treat review comments as the next editing pass rather than trying to perfect the draft before submission.

A secondary hedge: identify one or two other high-quality venues where the paper could go quickly if JAMIA comes back with a rejection rather than a revision — AMIA Annual Symposium proceedings (which have a shorter cycle and are respected in clinical informatics), or the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association's sister journal JAMIA Open if your findings are more observational than interventional.
